people.name: Darina Siv
body: In the late 1970s a young Cambodian woman escaped the Khmer Rouge and reached a refugee camp in Thailand. There Darina Siv met the man she would marry. In 1982 the couple moved to St. Paul.

Siv began her working life in Minnesota as a social worker, serving low-income Cambodian families. She went on to become executive director of the United Cambodian Association of Minnesota. Minnesota Public Radio reported her death in those terms in March 2002, calling her a longtime advocate for the Twin Cities Cambodian community.

Her advocacy reached the State Capitol. A tribute in the Congressional Record says she was instrumental in securing state legislation that helps foreign-born social workers overcome licensing barriers. That change reached beyond her own community, because it applied to foreign-born social workers from any country.
Siv also told her own story in print. Her memoir, Never Come Back: A Cambodian Woman's Journey, describes her personal hardships after the Khmer Rouge took control of Cambodia.
She died of cancer in March 2002 at age 44.
keyFacts: Late 1970s: Escaped the Khmer Rouge and reached a refugee camp in Thailand, where she met her husband.
1982: Settled in St. Paul.
Worked as a social worker, then became executive director of the United Cambodian Association of Minnesota.
Helped secure Minnesota legislation easing licensing barriers for foreign-born social workers.
Wrote the memoir Never Come Back: A Cambodian Woman's Journey.
March 2002: Died of cancer at age 44.
people.connectToWork: Which licensing or credential rules in your area keep a trained person from serving people in their own language, and who could you ask about changing them?

people.name: Sodanny Eir
body: On a stage at the Walker Art Center in 2021, dancers from Minnesota moved slowly in and out of formation as male and female deities in Robam Tep Monorom, the "Dance of Heavenly Bliss," set to music by the Royal Ballet of Cambodia. They were performing with the Wattanak Dance Troupe, which Sodanny Eir helped bring into being.

To see why that mattered, it helps to know what nearly happened to Cambodian classical dance. The Walker's curator wrote that nearly nine out of ten Cambodian classical dancers did not survive the Khmer Rouge regime. Survivors rebuilt the dances from memory.

Eir studied at the Royal University of Fine Arts in Phnom Penh. The Walker and Theater Mu both name Eir and Yousedy Peov as the troupe's founders in 2000. The troupe's own website dates its formal founding to 2008, names Peov as its founder, and describes Eir and Peov as the master teachers who trained its first dancers.

Little else about Eir's life has been published. The teaching she began can still be followed: Sarath Nob, now a co-artistic director of the troupe, began her formal training at seventeen under Eir and Peov.
keyFacts: Studied at the Royal University of Fine Arts, Phnom Penh.
Named as a co-founder of the Wattanak Dance Troupe by the Walker Art Center and Theater Mu, who date it to 2000.
Named as a master teacher by the troupe, which dates its formal founding to 2008.
2021: The troupe performed Robam Tep Monorom at the Walker's Choreographers' Evening.
people.connectToWork: When you read a founding date or a founder's name for a community group, how would you check whose account it is before you repeat it?

people.name: Yousedy Peov
body: Yousedy Peov is a dancer, master teacher and choreographer whose teaching sits at the root of the Wattanak Dance Troupe in Minnesota. Her father, You Leng Peov, was a playwright, theater director and educator.

After the Khmer Rouge fell, she trained at the Royal University of Fine Arts in Phnom Penh. In 1991 she joined Cambodia's Department of Fine Arts, and later that year the Royal Dance Troupe of the Cambodian Royal Ballet, and she performed internationally. After settling in Minnesota she taught and performed across the country.

The troupe began as a small group rehearsing at Watt Munisotaram in Hampton and is now based in Minneapolis. The Walker Art Center and Theater Mu date it to 2000, with Peov and Sodanny Eir as founders. The troupe's own website dates its formal founding to 2008, with Peov as founder.
Her students now lead the work. Garrett Sour, a co-artistic director, began training with her at six. In its 2026 listing the troupe reports more than 40 students enrolled in classes.
keyFacts: Trained at the Royal University of Fine Arts, Phnom Penh.
1991: Joined Cambodia's Department of Fine Arts, then the Royal Dance Troupe.
Founder of the Wattanak Dance Troupe; sources date it to 2000 or 2008.
Her students now direct the troupe.
people.connectToWork: Before asking someone to perform or share culture at your event, how would you find out what training and lineage they carry, and what fair recognition and payment would be?

people.name: Vichet Chhuon
body: In January 2018 Vichet Chhuon, a University of Minnesota professor, traveled to Cambodia with colleagues on a grant-funded project about families separated by U.S. immigration policy. They traveled with family members whose loved ones had been deported there.
Chhuon earned a Ph.D. at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is an associate professor in the University of Minnesota's Department of Curriculum and Instruction, as of October 2026.

His research asks how schools can better serve immigrant youth and students of color. His book Cambodian American Youth, Identity, and Schooling (Routledge, 2025) draws on two years of ethnographic research in one Southern California community.

In 2015 he received the Carl A. Grant Presidential Research Award from the National Association for Multicultural Education and the Early Career Achievement Award from the Association for Asian American Studies. On February 11, 2025, as a recipient of the Marty and Jack Rossmann award, he delivered the university's Rossmann Lecture, "Raids, Refugees, and Refusal: Cambodian American Resettlement and Deportation."

The Cambodia project also ran several rounds of teacher training workshops for people interested in teaching English there. Jenny Srey, who later co-wrote a book chapter with him, reached out to him during her husband's case because he was, in the words of the university's magazine, the only Cambodian professor in Minnesota she knew.
keyFacts: Ph.D., University of California, Santa Barbara.
Associate professor, Curriculum and Instruction, University of Minnesota.
2015: Carl A. Grant Presidential Research Award and Early Career Achievement Award.
January 2018: Traveled to Cambodia for a grant-funded project on family separation.
2025: Published Cambodian American Youth, Identity, and Schooling and delivered the Rossmann Lecture.

people.name: Jenny Srey
body: In 2016 Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Ched Nin, a Cambodian refugee in Minnesota who was not yet a U.S. citizen. He was one of eight men, known as the Minnesota Eight, whom MPR News described as rounded up for deportation to Cambodia. His wife, Jenny Srey, a 2006 University of Minnesota Family Social Science graduate, began organizing.

Some context helps here. MPR News reported that the men's families fled the Khmer Rouge, that most were born in refugee camps, and that most had served their prison sentences. A 1996 federal law made them subject to deportation, including for older convictions, and an immigration attorney told MPR that her clients had not understood their convictions would make them deportable.

Srey, a U.S. citizen, told MPR that deporting her husband was "the wrong thing to do." Working with community organizers, the University of Minnesota's College of Education and Human Development and the Law School's Center for New Americans, she co-founded Release MN8, which supported the eight men in custody. In late February 2017, after more than six months in detention, Nin was released when an immigration judge found his family would suffer extreme hardship if he were deported. His permanent residency was restored.

The work did not end with one family. The group, now Minnesota8, marked ten years in 2026 and is led by executive director Montha Chum. In a 2022 university profile Srey was described as a senior manager at the Coalition of Asian American Leaders, and she co-wrote a book chapter on this work with Vichet Chhuon and her husband.
keyFacts: 2006: Graduated from the University of Minnesota in Family Social Science.
2016: Her husband, Ched Nin, was arrested by ICE, one of the Minnesota Eight.
Co-founded Release MN8.
February 2017: Nin was released after a judge found deportation would cause his family extreme hardship.
2022: Described by the university as a senior manager at the Coalition of Asian American Leaders.
people.connectToWork: If a person hesitates to share immigration or family information with your program, what can you explain about who sees it and why, and what can you stop asking for?

people.name: Sokhary Chau
body: In January 2022 the Lowell, Massachusetts, City Council voted unanimously to choose its next mayor. Sokhary Chau had arrived in the United States as a child refugee. NBC News reported him as the first Cambodian American mayor in the country and the first Asian American mayor of Lowell.

His father, a captain in the Cambodian army, was executed by the Khmer Rouge in 1975. His mother kept her seven children alive and brought them out of Cambodia in the late 1970s. A Catholic church in Pittsburgh sponsored the family in 1981. They moved to Lowell for better-paying factory work, and he arrived there in 1986 at age 14.

His path ran through Minnesota. After a scholarship to Phillips Academy in Andover, he came to St. Paul for Macalester College and graduated in 1996 with a major in economics. He started a mortgage company, which closed after the 2008 crash, and later worked at law firms.

He lost his first run for the Lowell City Council in 2017 and won a seat in 2019. The mayor's office in Lowell is largely ceremonial: the mayor leads council meetings and chairs the school committee, while a city manager runs the city.

In 2026, as a city councilor, he challenged State Rep. Tara Hong, another Cambodian American, in the Democratic primary for the 18th Middlesex District on September 1. State election records show Hong winning, with 2,041 votes to 991 in the state's count.
keyFacts: 1975: His father was executed by the Khmer Rouge.
1981: Family sponsored by a Catholic church in Pittsburgh. 1986: Arrived in Lowell.
1996: Graduated from Macalester College in St. Paul.
2019: Elected to the Lowell City Council.
January 2022: Chosen mayor by a unanimous council vote.
September 1, 2026: Lost the Democratic primary for the Massachusetts House, 18th Middlesex District.
people.connectToWork: When a person has moved between states, what would you ask to learn which places and institutions shaped them, instead of assuming their story began here?

people.name: Dith Pran
body: As Phnom Penh fell to the Khmer Rouge in April 1975, Dith Pran was working as interpreter and assistant to New York Times correspondent Sydney Schanberg. Schanberg helped Dith's family leave the country, but Dith stayed behind. He survived by posing as an uneducated peasant, farming and eating very little, and escaped about four and a half years later. On his way out he passed clusters of corpses and skeletal remains. He gave those places a name the world still uses: the "killing fields."
Born in 1942 near the temples of Angkor Wat in Siem Reap, Dith became Schanberg's assistant in Phnom Penh before the takeover.

After his escape he resettled in the United States and worked as a photographer for The New York Times. Schanberg's 1980 magazine article, "The Death and Life of Dith Pran," became the basis of the 1984 film The Killing Fields.
Dith used that attention as a responsibility. He became a goodwill ambassador for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and founded the Dith Pran Holocaust Awareness Project.
He died of pancreatic cancer in New Jersey on March 30, 2008, at age 65.
keyFacts: 1942: Born in Siem Reap, Cambodia.
1975: Stayed behind after the Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh.
1979: Escaped to Thailand and coined the term "killing fields."
Worked as a New York Times photographer.
His story became the 1984 film The Killing Fields.
UN refugee agency goodwill ambassador; founded the Dith Pran Holocaust Awareness Project.
March 30, 2008: Died in New Jersey at age 65.
people.connectToWork: If an older person chooses not to talk about the years before they came here, what can your process get done without asking?

people.name: Haing S. Ngor
body: At the 1985 Academy Awards, a Cambodian doctor who had never trained as an actor accepted the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor. Haing S. Ngor had played Dith Pran in The Killing Fields, reenacting an era he had personally survived. He became only the second nonprofessional actor, after Harold Russell, to win an acting Oscar.

Sources give different birth years for Ngor, from 1940 to 1951; Encyclopedia.com calls 1947 the most common. He trained as a physician and practiced obstetrics and gynecology in Phnom Penh. He was a Khmer Rouge prisoner from 1975 to 1979, and his captors forced him to labor, starved and beat him, and cut off part of his little finger. His wife, Chang My Hoa, died in premature labor because, without surgical tools, he could not perform a cesarean section. In the fall of 1980 he settled in Los Angeles.
After the Oscar he spoke about the genocide and co-wrote the memoir A Cambodian Odyssey (1987) with Roger Warner. In the early 1990s he started a foundation under his name to support Cambodia.
On February 25, 1996, Ngor was shot and killed during a holdup outside his home in Los Angeles's Chinatown. In April 1998 three members of a local street gang were convicted of first-degree murder.
keyFacts: Before 1975: Practiced as an obstetrician-gynecologist in Phnom Penh.
1975–1979: Held prisoner by the Khmer Rouge.
1980: Settled in Los Angeles.
1985: Won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for The Killing Fields.
1987: Published A Cambodian Odyssey with Roger Warner.
February 25, 1996: Killed in Los Angeles.
people.connectToWork: What skills or professional life might a person have had before arriving that your intake form never asks about, and how would you ask?

people.name: Sichan Siv
body: In 1975, as the Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities, Sichan Siv left his family and rode a bicycle for about three weeks across the country before he was captured. On February 13, 1976, he jumped from a logging truck and spent three days crossing mined and patrolled jungle to Thailand. He taught English to fellow refugees in a camp there. He later learned that his mother, older sister, older brother and their families had been killed. Of the 16 relatives who left Phnom Penh together on April 17, 1975, he was the only survivor.

He reached the United States on June 4, 1976, and was resettled in Connecticut. He worked jobs including apple picker and taxi driver, then earned a Master of International Affairs at Columbia University.

From 1989 to 1993 he served at the White House as Deputy Assistant to President George H. W. Bush and at the State Department as a Deputy Assistant Secretary. He was later unanimously confirmed by the Senate and served as a U.S. ambassador to the United Nations from 2001 to 2006 under President George W. Bush.

His memoir, Golden Bones (2008), takes its title from an old Cambodian saying that a very lucky child is born with golden bones. His own biography, checked in October 2026, lists him as a member of the Texas Board of Criminal Justice.
keyFacts: 1975: Crossed Cambodia by bicycle before being captured.
February 13, 1976: Escaped, reaching Thailand, and taught English in a refugee camp.
The only survivor of 16 family members who left Phnom Penh together.
Earned a Master of International Affairs from Columbia University.
1989–1993: Deputy Assistant to President George H. W. Bush.
2001–2006: U.S. ambassador to the United Nations.
2008: Published the memoir Golden Bones.
people.connectToWork: If a person's first jobs here look nothing like their abilities, how does your process avoid judging what they can do from those jobs alone?

people.name: Loung Ung
body: Loung Ung was five years old when the Khmer Rouge marched into Phnom Penh in April 1975. Her father led the family out of the city on foot. During the flight her fifteen-year-old sister died of food poisoning, and the Khmer Rouge took her father, who was never seen again. In 1977 her mother sent the children away to pose as orphans in camps that trained them as combatants. Ung later learned that her mother and youngest sister had been murdered.

After Vietnamese forces entered Cambodia she reached a refugee camp in Thailand. A charitable organization sponsored her, a brother and his wife, and they settled in Vermont around 1980. Other relatives stayed in Cambodia.

Ung turned her childhood into testimony. First They Killed My Father: A Daughter of Cambodia Remembers (2000) tells the story of the genocide through a child's eyes. Lucky Child (2005) follows her life in America alongside that of the sister she left behind. Angelina Jolie directed a 2017 Netflix film of the first book.
From 1997 to 2003 she worked with the Vietnam Veterans of America Foundation and served as a national spokesperson in the campaign to ban landmines.
keyFacts: 1970: Born in Phnom Penh.
1975–1979: Lost her parents and two sisters during the Khmer Rouge years.
About 1980: Settled in Vermont with a brother and his wife.
2000: Published First They Killed My Father. 2005: Published Lucky Child.
1997–2003: Worked on the campaign to ban landmines.
2017: Netflix film directed by Angelina Jolie.
people.connectToWork: When you ask who is in a person's family or household, how does your form make room for close relatives who live in another country?

people.name: Anthony Veasna So
body: In August 2021 a debut story collection called Afterparties arrived in bookstores. Its setting was Cambodian American life in California's Central Valley. Its author, Anthony Veasna So, did not live to see it published. He died on December 8, 2020, at age 28.

So was a native of Stockton, California. He graduated from Stanford University and earned an MFA in fiction at Syracuse University. He taught at Syracuse, at Colgate University and at the Center for Empowering Refugees and Immigrants in Oakland. In February 2020 The New Yorker published his story "Three Women of Chuck's Donuts," about a Cambodian immigrant family running a struggling business during the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis.
He wrote about the children who grew up in America after the genocide, with humor as well as grief.

Afterparties, published by Ecco, won the National Book Critics Circle's John Leonard Prize for best first book and the Ferro-Grumley Award for LGBTQ fiction, and was long-listed for the Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence in Fiction.
keyFacts: 1992: Born; a native of Stockton, California.
Graduated from Stanford University; MFA in fiction from Syracuse University.
Taught at Colgate, Syracuse and the Center for Empowering Refugees and Immigrants in Oakland.
December 8, 2020: Died at age 28.
2021: Afterparties published by Ecco.
Won the John Leonard Prize and the Ferro-Grumley Award.
people.connectToWork: If a person grew up here as the child of refugees, what would you ask them rather than assuming their parents' history is, or is not, part of their life?

people.name: Arn Chorn-Pond
body: In 1984 a teenager stood before 10,000 people at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York and described what he had lived through as a child in Cambodia. By the account of Cambodian Living Arts, Arn Chorn-Pond was the first Cambodian child soldier to speak publicly about the atrocities of the genocide.

He was born in 1966 into a family of performers and musicians from Battambang. Under the Khmer Rouge he was sent to a children's labor camp, where he survived by playing his flute for the guards. He fled in 1979 and reached a refugee camp in Thailand, where the Rev. Peter Pond, a Lutheran minister and aid worker, adopted him in 1980 and brought him to New Hampshire. He attended Brown University and graduated from Providence College.

Much of his early advocacy happened in the United States. He founded Children of War and Peace Makers, a gang-intervention program for Southeast Asian youth in Providence, and co-founded the Southeast Asian Big Brothers/Big Sisters of America Association. He also directed youth programs for the Cambodian Mutual Assistance Association in Lowell, Massachusetts. His honors include the Reebok Human Rights Award (1988), the Amnesty International Human Rights Award (1991), the Kohl Foundation International Peace Prize (1993) and the Spirit of Anne Frank Outstanding Citizen Award (1996).

When he returned to Cambodia he looked for the master musicians and performers who had survived. In 1998 he founded what is now Cambodian Living Arts, with five students learning from those masters. He lives outside Phnom Penh. His story is the subject of Patricia McCormick's novel Never Fall Down (2012), and he appears in the documentary The Flute Player.
keyFacts: 1966: Born in Battambang to a family of performers.
Survived a Khmer Rouge children's camp by playing his flute for the guards.
1980: Adopted by Rev. Peter Pond; moved to New Hampshire.
1984: Spoke publicly about the genocide at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine.
Founded Children of War and Peace Makers.
1988–1996: Reebok, Amnesty International, Kohl Foundation and Spirit of Anne Frank honors.
1998: Founded Cambodian Living Arts with five students.

people.name: Rady Mom
body: On election night in November 2014, a 45-year-old acupressure therapist in Lowell, Massachusetts, won the 18th Middlesex House District with more than 61 percent of the vote. Rady Mom became, as Boston press and others reported, the first Cambodian American state legislator in the country.

Mom was born in 1970 in Pailin, in northwestern Cambodia. The Khmer Rouge took his father, a village chief. Mom lived in a refugee camp as a child and left Cambodia with his family at about 12. Sources differ on when he reached the United States: a 2014 Boston magazine profile says 1982 and VOA says 1984. His path ran through Minnesota. By his own account in Working Immigrants, the Chester Park church in Duluth sponsored his family and 34 others, and the family moved from Duluth to Lowell in 1984.
Before running for office he was active in Lowell's Cambodian Mutual Assistance Association, the Angkor Dance Troupe and the Khmer Cultural Council.

He won contested primaries in 2016 and 2018 and ran unopposed in 2020. He told GBH he had not set out to make history but to represent his community. He held the seat from 2015 to 2025, when it passed to another Cambodian American, Tara Hong, who defeated him in 2024.
keyFacts: 1970: Born in Pailin, Cambodia.
Early 1980s: Came to the U.S. as a refugee; sponsored by a church in Duluth, Minnesota.
1984: The family moved from Duluth to Lowell.
Active with the Cambodian Mutual Assistance Association, Angkor Dance Troupe and Khmer Cultural Council.
November 2014: Elected to the Massachusetts House, reported as the first Cambodian American state legislator.
2024: Lost the seat to Tara Hong; served until 2025.

people.name: Ted Ngoy
body: In 1975 a cargo plane from Cambodia landed at Camp Pendleton in Southern California carrying a family of five fleeing war. Within a few years the father, Ted Ngoy, would build a chain of doughnut shops.

Peace Lutheran Church in Tustin sponsored the family, and Ngoy cared for the church grounds until he found a job with a doughnut chain. He learned the business, bought a shop in La Habra with the family's savings and built a string of shops along the coast.
He then leased shops to other Cambodian refugees, which is how his story reached well past his own family. He also became influential in local and national politics.

His story is not a simple success story. Orange Coast magazine reports that he developed a gambling addiction and lost his wealth, his marriage and his standing. He returned to Cambodia and ran a failed political campaign, and a 2005 Los Angeles Times profile described him as broke and homeless. By 2018 he was selling real estate in Cambodia and had published a memoir, The Donut King: The Rags to Riches Story of a Poor Immigrant Who Changed the World. Alice Gu's documentary The Donut King received a Special Jury Recognition at the 2020 SXSW Film Festival.
keyFacts: 1975: Arrived at Camp Pendleton with his family; sponsored by Peace Lutheran Church, Tustin.
Bought his first doughnut shop in La Habra, then built a chain.
Leased shops to Cambodian refugee families.
Later lost his fortune to gambling addiction and returned to Cambodia.
2018: Published the memoir The Donut King.
2020: Subject of Alice Gu's documentary The Donut King.
people.connectToWork: How does your program respond when someone who once did very well now needs help, and what would make it easier for them to ask?

people.name: Kalyanee Mam
body: In January 2013, at the Sundance Film Festival, the documentary A River Changes Course won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize. Sundance described it as following three young Cambodians struggling to overcome deforestation, overfishing and overwhelming debt. Its director, Kalyanee Mam, had been born in that country during its darkest years.
Mam was born in Battambang under the Khmer Rouge and moved to the United States with her family in 1981.

Before directing her own feature she worked as a cinematographer on the Oscar-winning documentary Inside Job. A River Changes Course also won the Golden Gate Award for Best Feature Documentary at the San Francisco International Film Festival.

She went on to co-direct and co-produce Between Earth & Sky and to make Lost World, which screened at Mountainfilm in 2019. Her films look at what Cambodians are living through now, not only at the genocide.
keyFacts: Born in Battambang under the Khmer Rouge.
1981: Moved to the U.S. with her family.
Cinematographer on Inside Job.
2013: A River Changes Course won the Sundance World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for Documentary and the Golden Gate Award.
2019: Lost World screened at Mountainfilm.

people.name: Sophiline Cheam Shapiro
body: In 2009 the National Endowment for the Arts named Sophiline Cheam Shapiro a National Heritage Fellow. The dancer who received it had once been a child sent to do farm labor under the Khmer Rouge.

When the regime took power in 1975, her family was driven from the city to the countryside, where she was assigned work such as collecting cow dung for fertilizer. She lost her father and two brothers. After the regime fell she returned to the city, began training at the School of Fine Arts in Phnom Penh, and in 1988 graduated with the first generation of classical dancers trained after the Khmer Rouge. She then taught there for three years.

The NEA's biography and Northrop at the University of Minnesota both say she moved to Southern California in 1991, and Northrop says she studied dance ethnology at UCLA. In 2002 she co-founded the Khmer Arts Academy in Long Beach, and in 2006 she established a center in Cambodia.

She has made new work as well as preserving the classical repertoire. Samritechak (2000) adapts Shakespeare's Othello as Cambodian classical dance, and later works include Seasons of Migration (2005) and Pamina Devi (2006). Her honors include the Nikkei Asia Prize for Culture and Guggenheim and Irvine fellowships.
keyFacts: 1975–1979: Forced into rural labor; lost her father and two brothers.
1988: Graduated from the dance program in Phnom Penh, then taught there.
1991: Moved to Southern California; studied dance ethnology at UCLA.
2002: Co-founded the Khmer Arts Academy in Long Beach.
2009: NEA National Heritage Fellowship.

people.name: Rithy Hanh
body: As of the agency's January 2024 article, Rithy Hanh was a senior advocate at Disability Rights California, the state's protection and advocacy agency, and its first Khmer-speaking employee who can also read and write Khmer. He co-wrote that article, on reaching Cambodian communities.

He was born in a refugee camp on the Cambodia-Thailand border and lived there for 11 years. In his article he says he wants to connect the Cambodian and disability communities and build relationships with APSARA and other Cambodian organizations across California. In August 2023 he arranged for four Cambodian community members from Long Beach to speak at a Disability Rights California board meeting, and he demonstrated a traditional Cambodian dance there. "If we can empower one family," he said, "that one family will continue to empower each other."
keyFacts: January 2024: Senior advocate at Disability Rights California, by the agency's article of that date.
The article calls him the agency's first Khmer-speaking employee who can also read and write Khmer.
Born in a refugee camp on the Cambodia-Thailand border.
January 2024: Co-wrote an article on outreach to Cambodian communities.
people.connectToWork: Does anyone on your team read and write the languages your program serves, and if not, who checks what your materials actually say?

people.name: Samith Mey
body: Samith Mey is the founder and executive director of the Phnom Penh Center for Independent Living in Cambodia, established in 2009 by Cambodians with disabilities. He signs the center's message from its executive director, which was checked in October 2026.

In a 2019 forum talk he said he was born in 1979 and has polio. He trained in independent living through Japan's Duskin Leadership Training program in 2006 and 2007. He described the center as the only independent living center in Cambodia, offering peer counseling, independent living programs and personal assistant services. The Zero Project recognized its introduction of a personal assistance model.
His work is based in Cambodia, not Minnesota. It shows a Khmer-led independent living movement that exists on its own terms.
keyFacts: Born 1979; has said he has polio.
2006–2007: Duskin Leadership Training in Japan.
2009: Center established; he is its founder and executive director.
The Zero Project recognized the center's personal assistance model.

institutions.name: Watt Munisotaram
institutions.location: 2925 220th Street East, between Hampton and Farmington, Dakota County, Minnesota (the temple's website gives the city as Empire)
body: Drive about 30 miles south of the Twin Cities into farm country and golden spires rise among the fields. Watt Munisotaram is a Theravada Buddhist temple started by Cambodian refugees who fled the Khmer Rouge. AP reports that its name roughly means the place to enjoy learning from wise men.

MNopedia dates the congregation to 1982, when a small group of refugees set out to start a monastery and the main Buddhist temple in Washington, D.C., sent the Venerable Chey Siddhi San as first abbot. Services began in a rented house in Minneapolis, moved to St. Paul in 1984 and to Eagan in 1988, and that year the Minnesota Cambodian Buddhist Society bought land in Dakota County.

Construction of the main temple began in 2002 on a design by architect Yav Socchea. MPR News reported that it took five years and about $1.5 million, and that thousands attended its consecration in July 2007. Rochester also has a Cambodian Buddhist temple, Watt Dhamma Visudhikaram at 4462 29th St. SE, which KIMT (2025) says has served a Rochester Cambodian community of more than 800 for over 20 years. In 2025 the temple unveiled a Great Gate that took six years of fundraising and cost more than $1 million.

The 40-acre site holds golden Buddha statues, a stupa and a meditation pond. In 2023 AP reported that ten monks live there. Rehearsals for Wattanak Dance Troupe once took place at the temple. MNopedia records events such as Khmer New Year and Visakha Puja, and in the temple's own words public hours are Thursday to Sunday.
keyFacts: 1982: Congregation formed.
1988: Land bought in Dakota County.
July 2007: Main temple consecrated, with thousands attending.
About 40 acres, about 30 miles south of the Twin Cities.
2025: Great Gate unveiled.
As of 2025, Iddhimuni Moeng Sang is abbot and head monk, according to Sahan Journal.
institutions.connectToWork: If you want to work with a temple, who would you ask first about how and when to approach it, and how would you make sure the person you serve wants that connection?

institutions.name: National Cambodian Heritage Museum & Killing Fields Memorial
aliases: Cambodian American Heritage Museum and Killing Fields Memorial
body: Inside a building on Chicago's North Side, back-lit glass panels carry the names of people killed in the Cambodian genocide. WBEZ reported in 2009 that the memorial has 80 panels, each representing 25,000 people. Clio says the list of names continues to grow.

The museum grew out of the Cambodian Association of Illinois, formed in 1976 as a chapter of the Cambodian Association of America and independent since 1983. The association bought the building on Lawrence Avenue in 1998 and raised more than a million dollars for construction and renovation. The museum opened in 2004 as the Cambodian American Heritage Museum and Killing Fields Memorial. In 2015 it was incorporated as its own entity, while remaining part of the association, and took its current name.

The International Coalition of Sites of Conscience, of which it is a member, says it offers exhibitions and resources on Cambodian history and culture, works to raise awareness of the genocide and celebrate the renewal of Cambodian community and culture in the United States, and provides a peaceful place where survivors can gather and heal. The memorial honors the roughly two million Cambodians who died from 1975 to 1979. By Clio's account it is the first permanent monument to those victims. Its 2026 annual fundraiser took place on October 10.
keyFacts: 1976: Cambodian Association of Illinois formed; independent since 1983.
1998: Building on Lawrence Avenue purchased.
2004: Museum and memorial opened.
2015: Incorporated separately and renamed.
The Wall of Remembrance lists names of victims on back-lit glass panels.

institutions.name: United Cambodian Association of Minnesota
institutions.type: Mutual assistance and social services organization
institutions.location: 1385 Mendota Heights Road, Suite 500, Mendota Heights, Minnesota
body: According to its own account, the United Cambodian Association of Minnesota formed in January 1993 when the Khmer Association of Minnesota merged with the Refugee and Immigrant Resource Center, to reduce duplicated services and competition for funding. It describes itself as the only human service organization in Minnesota dedicated to the social service needs of Cambodian immigrants and refugees.

Its program areas are elders, families, youth, health and legal services. Since October 2014 it has run an Adult Day Services program, supervised daytime care for older adults or people with disabilities, covering Anoka, Carver, Dakota, Hennepin, Ramsey, Scott and Washington counties. It also lists scholarships, mentorship, language classes and cultural events.
Darina Siv, profiled on this page, was its executive director when she died in 2002.
keyFacts: January 1993: Formed by the merger of the Khmer Association of Minnesota and the Refugee and Immigrant Resource Center.
Program areas: elders, families, youth, health and legal services.
October 2014: Adult Day Services opened; covers seven metro counties.
Darina Siv was executive director at her death in 2002.

institutions.name: Asian Pacific Self-Development and Residential Association
institutions.type: Grassroots membership organization, housing and services
body: In 1989, 35 Cambodian refugee families founded APSARA in Stockton, California. In 1993 the group bought the 230-unit Park Village Apartments from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for one dollar. Disability Rights California, the source of this account, says APSARA means "dancer" in Khmer and offers housing along with early literacy, youth leadership and senior wellness programs.

In a January 2024 Disability Rights California article, Rithy Hanh, also on this page, said he hopes to build relationships with APSARA and other Cambodian organizations to better support Cambodians with disabilities. The article describes no formal partnership. APSARA's program manager, Sothea Ung, told the agency that trauma acts like a magnet that pulls people backward, making past events feel recent. APSARA is not specific to disability and is not in Minnesota.
keyFacts: 1989: Founded by 35 refugee families in Stockton.
1993: Bought its 230-unit apartment complex from HUD.
Offers housing, early literacy, youth leadership and senior wellness programs.
Named by Disability Rights California as a group it hopes to work with.
institutions.connectToWork: Which groups near you were founded by the people they serve, and what would they need to gain before a partnership with your agency was worth their time?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It describes no person or family. The sources cited here provide limited research on how Cambodian Americans understand disability and do not include a disability study specific to Minnesota. Two Minnesota studies on related topics are noted below. What follows comes from one small U.S. interview study of parents, an advocacy agency's outreach article, older studies of Cambodian refugees and mental health (including one Minnesota thesis), and a report written about Cambodia, not about U.S. families. Views differ by generation, time in the U.S., faith and education. On this page, Cambodian and Khmer refer to people who identify that way, including people of other faiths and backgrounds.
questions: What do you think is going on, and what does it mean for you and your family, if you would like to say?
Who gave you a label or diagnosis, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open for you, and what do you want it to avoid?
Who, if anyone, would you like involved in decisions, such as a spouse, parents, elders or a monk?
Do you use help from a temple, a monk or a kru khmer, and how should our services work alongside it?
Which words do you use for this, in Khmer and in English?
Would you like a Khmer interpreter, and is there anyone you would rather not have as your interpreter?
What would you like to share about the past, if anything, and what would you rather we not ask?
What support from family, community or temple do you want us to build on?
Would a group or an activity with peers be useful to you?

context.heading: What the research on families shows, and does not
body: In a 2024 interview study of 11 Khmer-speaking Cambodian American parents of children with disabilities, parents held differing views on what disability means and what causes it. No one explanation fits them all. The abstract names the authors' university, UMass Lowell, and does not state a study site. This account rests on the published abstract.

Disability Rights California wrote in 2024 that disability is often stigmatized in Cambodian culture and that, in the Buddhist faith, a child's disability may be seen as a sign of bad karma, which can cause shame and keep families from services. That is one agency's outreach article, not a study.

A report by Charles Conklin of Mennonite Central Committee, first published in 2023, says mothers in Cambodia are often blamed for a child's disability and expected to be the main caregiver, and also that more Cambodians are turning to medical care. It describes Cambodia, not U.S. families. No study of how this applies in Minnesota was found.

sources.label: Werunga, Kim and Rosales, Journal of Southeast Asian American Education and Advancement (2024), abstract
Disability Rights California, "Building Connections with the Cambodian Community" (2024)
Conklin, Anabaptist Disabilities Network, "Disability, Safeguarding, and Inclusion in Cambodia"

context.heading: Trauma, health care and what helped
body: A 2020 University of Washington thesis gathered 3 focus groups and 30 interviews with 50 Cambodian Americans aged 19 to 75 in the Seattle area. It found three themes: difficulty navigating the health system, sociocultural influences, and historical trauma, which it links to conditions such as PTSD and to whether people use care. Participants showed a preference for wellness activities with peers. The author recommends services that avoid re-traumatizing people.

Disability Rights California cites a 2005 RAND study finding that nearly two-thirds of Cambodian adults studied had PTSD about 20 years after the Khmer Rouge period. The article gives no sample or place, so do not read it as a rate for any group here, and never as a fact about a person. Ask what produced an impairment only as a question the person may choose to answer.

In the 2024 parent study, language and cultural differences were challenges, and knowing more about special education tended to increase parent involvement. Disability Rights California names Khmer-speaking staff as part of its approach. Use a trained interpreter, not a child, and remember that a small community can make privacy harder.

sources.label: Than, University of Washington thesis (2020)
Disability Rights California, "Building Connections with the Cambodian Community" (2024)
Werunga, Kim and Rosales, Journal of Southeast Asian American Education and Advancement (2024), abstract

context.heading: Monks, healers and formal services
body: A 1987 University of Washington dissertation interviewed most members of ten Cambodian extended families in Pierce County, Washington, along with Buddhist monks, kru khmer and other healers. Participants mainly attributed mental illness to a weakened spirit after the death of or separation from family. Healing included strengthening family ties, Buddhist practice, exorcism and magical protection, and this group found Western therapists less effective than traditional healers. The study is nearly 40 years old and covers one county.

A 1996 Augsburg College thesis in Minnesota studied one Buddhist monk and one kru healer. The monk advised that social workers who understand family roles and religious beliefs are better prepared to help. The healer said he would not recommend Western professionals to his clients. The author concluded that teamwork across these approaches takes time, patience and flexibility. Two people cannot stand for a community. Ask about temple or healer support without judging it, and plan services to work alongside what the person chooses.

sources.label: Duncan, University of Washington dissertation (1987)
Thach, Augsburg College thesis (1996)

context.heading: Words, and what could not be found
body: Disability Rights California says Khmer has no word for autism, so explain a diagnosis in plain language rather than only translating it, and check what was understood.
No published Khmer terms for disability, terms people find hurtful, or preferred respectful terms were found, so none are offered. Ask the person and the interpreter which words to use.

No source was found on how decisions about disability services are made in Cambodian American families. No Minnesota organization specific to Khmer disability was found, though the search was limited. A University of Minnesota CURA project with MN8 and Wilder Research built a needs assessment of Cambodian Minnesotans in 2021 and 2022, covering immigration, food insecurity, health insurance and language. Wilder Research published the findings in June 2022: 18 interviews on language and literacy, food, health coverage, voting and immigration, with recommendations for culturally specific mental health services and stigma reduction. A 2010 University of Minnesota study (Lee, Lytle, Yang and Lum, International Journal of Aging and Human Development 71(4)) examined depression literacy among Hmong and Cambodian elders in the Twin Cities through focus groups with nine professionals. Neither is a disability study as such, but both are specific to Minnesota.

communityRoutes.name: United Cambodian Association of Minnesota, Adult Day Services
communityRoutes.purpose: Supervised daytime care for older adults or people with disabilities, with health, social and nutrition support, in Anoka, Carver, Dakota, Hennepin, Ramsey, Scott and Washington counties. Its site says coverage may come from waivers, the Alternative Care Program, TRICARE, long-term care insurance or private pay. Ask the person first whether they want this connection.

communityRoutes.name: Khmer Health Advocates
communityRoutes.purpose: A Connecticut nonprofit founded in 1982 by Theanvy Kuoch, with community health workers and psychiatrist-led programs that, as reported in 2022, have supported 1,700 Cambodian Americans. Outside Minnesota; a possible source of practice knowledge for providers.

organizations.intro: Sahan Journal reported in November 2025, citing Minnesota Compass, that about 12,000 Cambodians live in Minnesota, mostly in and around the Twin Cities. The article gives no margin of error, and it is one estimate of a small population. Cambodian Minnesotans have built temples, churches, service agencies, arts groups and advocacy groups. No Minnesota-based Khmer-language radio station, newspaper or television program was found. National and international outlets are listed for reference. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Cambodian American Partnership of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A nonprofit that says it works to uplift and preserve Cambodian culture, arts and history through community partnership. It has run Cambodian Heritage Day and a gala; its site lists 2025 events.

entries.name: Minnesota8
entries.purpose: Says it fights to end detention and deportation in Southeast Asian communities, through organizing, advocacy, direct support and leadership development, with a youth program. Grew out of the campaign for eight Cambodian Minnesotans detained in 2016. Montha Chum is executive director, as MPR News reported in August 2026.

entries.name: Wattanak Dance Troupe
entries.purpose: Teaches and performs Cambodian classical and folk dance. Its site reports more than 40 students in classes. Yousedy Peov and Sodanny Eir are profiled on this page.

entries.name: Cambodian Church of the Nazarene
aliases: Minneapolis Cambodian Church of the Nazarene
entries.purpose: A Cambodian congregation listed by the City of Crystal as Mpls Cambodian Church of the Nazarene, 6421 45th Ave. N., 763-537-7878. Call to confirm service times.

entries.name: Cambodian Student Association of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Founded in 1988. Student volunteering, mentoring and Cambodian culture. University of Minnesota Asian American Studies lists it among current student groups, though the group's own site was last updated around 2019, so check with the university first.
entries.linkLabel: University of Minnesota list of Asian American student organizations

entries.name: Watt Munisotaram on Facebook
entries.purpose: The temple's own page for events and announcements, in Khmer and English.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota immigrants and communities of color, including recent stories on Cambodian Minnesotans. Multicultural, not specific to Cambodian communities.

entries.name: SEARAC
entries.purpose: Founded in 1979. A national civil rights organization working with communities from Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam on data equity, health, mental health and aging, education and immigration.

entries.name: Khmer Health Advocates
entries.purpose: Founded in 1982. Community health workers and programs for survivors of torture, along with research on trauma and chronic illness. Described here from 2022 coverage.

entries.name: Cambodian Association of America
entries.purpose: Counseling, including geriatric and caregiver counseling, parenting classes, kinship care support, substance use treatment, job readiness and help with health coverage.

entries.name: The Cambodian Family
entries.location: Santa Ana, California, 1626 East Fourth Street
entries.purpose: Serving refugee and immigrant families since 1980 through youth, community health and mental health, citizenship and civic engagement programs.

entries.name: United Cambodian Community
entries.location: Long Beach, California, 2201 East Anaheim Street, Suite 200
entries.purpose: Established in 1977 by a small group of Cambodian refugees. Programs in health equity, youth, community integration and economic development. It organized Long Beach Cambodian Restaurant Week in May 2026.

entries.name: Cambodian Living Arts
entries.purpose: Founded by Arn Chorn-Pond, profiled on this page. Offers grants, community arts outreach, scholarships and fiscal sponsorship for Cambodian artists.

entries.name: Khmer Post USA
entries.purpose: Founded in Philadelphia in 2005; moved to Lowell in 2010. Cambodian American and Cambodia news, free and supported by advertising. VOA reported in 2024 that it faced financial strain.

entries.name: Khmer TV
entries.purpose: Describes itself as a television station for Cambodian Americans. Its YouTube channel shows about 125,000 subscribers.

entries.name: RFA Khmer
entries.purpose: News on Cambodia. Radio Free Asia announced in October 2025 that it was suspending editorial operations, yet its Khmer site was carrying stories dated October 30, 2026, when checked. Its funding is uncertain.

entries.name: Khmer Times
entries.purpose: Launched in May 2014 and owned by Virtus Media. The paper says it is neutral; Lingua Sinica reports outside descriptions of it as strongly favoring the ruling party.
entries.linkLabel: Lingua Sinica profile of Khmer Times

entries.name: Cambodian Television Network
entries.purpose: Launched in March 2003. The Media Ownership Monitor reports a 30 percent audience share from a 2015 source and U.S. distribution as CTN International beginning in 2004. The sources found do not show whether that U.S. feed still runs.

entries.name: CamboJA News
entries.purpose: Published by the Cambodian Journalists Alliance Association, in English and Khmer. Describes itself as independent news from Cambodia.

entries.name: Kiripost
entries.purpose: Cambodia news, business and technology, in English and Khmer. Signed a joint press freedom statement with other media groups in April 2026.
